title: Inventory the available network tools
command: command -v ip ss ping traceroute mtr fping arp-scan netdiscover nmap ncat tcpdump tshark wireshark nping hping3 iperf3 smbclient ssh-audit
explanation: Check what is installed before following an exercise.
options: Missing output for a name usually means it is not on PATH. Use official Kali package information rather than assuming executable and package names match.

title: Identify interfaces and IPv4/IPv6 addresses
explanation: Match the interface to your VM adapter before choosing capture or probe targets.
options: The brief view shows administrative/link state and assigned addresses. An interface can be up without a usable route. A virtual Ethernet adapter is not a wireless radio.

title: Ask which route would be used
command:
ip route get 192.0.2.10
ip -6 route show
explanation: Route lookup explains which interface and source address a connection would use.
options: The IPv4 address is an example owned lab host, not a discovered device. route get calculates a route without sending a probe; IPv6 routing needs separate review.
result: A route decision or unreachable diagnostic.

title: Inspect listening ports and processes
explanation: Local socket inspection answers what is listening before you scan remotely.
options: -l listeners, -n numeric, -t TCP, -u UDP, -p process details. 127.0.0.1 differs from 0.0.0.0; a listener can still be blocked remotely by a firewall.
result: Ports, bind addresses and processes where permissions allow.

title: Test loopback with a small ping
explanation: Confirm local IPv4 and IPv6 ICMP behavior.
options: -c limits requests; -W sets IPv4 response wait here. Success tests loopback, not internet access. Missing replies from a remote host can reflect filtering.

title: Compare two explicit lab hosts with fping
explanation: Check a short approved inventory rather than a guessed subnet.
options: Replace both addresses with owned lab systems. -c sets attempts per host; -t is timeout in milliseconds. Results are reachability observations, not vulnerability findings.

title: Inspect a short path with traceroute
explanation: Observe routers that return TTL-expiry replies toward your lab host.
options: -n avoids reverse DNS, -m caps hops, -q uses one probe per hop, -w limits reply wait. Asterisks are missing replies, not proof of a broken forward path.

title: Use mtr for repeated path observations
explanation: Combine repeated probes with a route-style report.
options: -r report mode; -c five cycles. Intermediate-hop loss that does not continue to later hops often reflects reply throttling, not application packet loss.

title: Read the neighbor cache
command:
ip neigh show
ip -6 neigh show
explanation: Inspect recently learned local-link neighbors.
options: ARP supports IPv4 neighbor resolution; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery. STALE is a cache state, not a claim that the host is offline.
result: Cached neighbors; this is not a complete live inventory.

title: Discover one local-link lab host with ARP
explanation: Send ARP requests on the explicitly selected lab interface.
options: Replace eth1 after inspecting ip -br address. ARP stays on the local layer-2 segment and does not discover routed subnets. Vendor labels from MAC prefixes are hints.
result: An IPv4/MAC observation if the host replies.

title: Observe ARP traffic with Netdiscover
explanation: Passive mode observes ARP traffic visible on the chosen lab link.
options: -p disables active probes. Replace eth1 with the lab interface. Wait for ordinary traffic, then q exits. Silence is not proof there are no devices; switches limit visibility.

title: Connect discovery to the Nmap chapter
explanation: Assess only three relevant services on an owned lab host.
options: -sT connects, -sV attempts identification. See Chapter 19 for scan states, UDP ambiguity, scripts and XML reports. A service label without strong evidence can be wrong.
result: Port states and possible service details.

title: Record a segmentation test matrix
command:
Source zone | Destination asset | Protocol/port | Expected | Observed
Lab client | Test server | TCP/443 | Allow | Pending
Lab client | Management interface | TCP/22 | Deny | Pending
Management VM | Test server | TCP/22 | Allow | Pending
explanation: Segmentation testing compares actual reachability with a documented policy.
options: Test a known listening service from each approved vantage point. Check IPv4 and IPv6 separately. A closed port cannot prove a firewall denied access; correlate device logs and local listeners.
result: A reproducible policy matrix with evidence.

title: Create a network evidence folder
explanation: Keep captures and notes together.
options: Use synthetic traffic in these exercises. Raw captures may contain credentials or application data; store and share them according to their contents.

title: Ncat: start a loopback text listener
explanation: A plain TCP listener lets you see what a connection transports.
options: Keep Terminal A open. Binding explicitly to loopback avoids listening on the LAN. This accepts a text connection and does not launch a shell.
result: A waiting listener; use the next example in Terminal B.

title: Ncat: connect and exchange text
explanation: Connect to the preceding listener and type hello lab followed by Enter.
options: Text appears in the other terminal. Type a reply there to observe both directions. Ctrl+C ends the exercise. Ncat and other nc implementations have different options.

title: Capture a short loopback exercise
explanation: Start this before the Ncat client, then exchange synthetic text.
options: -i lo captures loopback; -nn suppresses lookups; -s 0 retains full packets; -c caps packets. timeout stops after 20 seconds even if fewer arrive. Exit 124 can indicate the planned timeout.
result: A bounded capture file, replacing that filename.

title: Read the capture with tcpdump
explanation: Review saved evidence without capturing again.
options: -r reads a file. Identify handshake flags, payload lengths and connection closure. A zero-packet capture may mean capture started too late or used the wrong interface.
result: A packet summary from the saved file.

title: TShark: show selected packet fields
command: tshark -r "$HOME/kali-lab/network/local.pcap" -Y 'tcp.port == 9099' -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.dstport -e tcp.len
explanation: Extract a compact table for review.
options: -r is offline input; -Y is a display filter; -T fields selects fields. IPv6 packets require ipv6.src rather than ip.src.

title: TShark: inspect TCP analysis flags
explanation: Find packets the dissector considers retransmitted or out of order.
options: A small loopback exercise may produce no matches. Capture loss, offloading and vantage point affect these heuristics; a flagged packet alone does not establish a network fault.

title: Wireshark: follow the training connection
command:
Open local.pcap in Wireshark.
Apply: tcp.port == 9099
Select a packet > Follow > TCP Stream.
Compare the two directions of text.
explanation: Following a stream helps relate packet fragments to application data.
options: Use the file created by the capture exercise. This plaintext example is visible; encrypted application content will not automatically be readable. No need to run the GUI as root.

title: Capinfos: summarize capture metadata
explanation: Check packet count, capture period and file properties before drawing conclusions.
options: Metadata describes the captured file, not all traffic that occurred. Record clock quality and the capture interface in separate notes.

title: Editcap: make a small review copy
explanation: Select the first ten captured packets into a separate file.
options: With -r, specified packet numbers are retained. The original remains available. Selecting fewer packets is not redaction; any retained payload remains in the copy.

title: Scapy: construct a packet without sending
command:
python3 - <<'PY'
from scapy.all import IP, ICMP, raw
p = IP(dst='127.0.0.1') / ICMP()
p.show()
print('Serialized bytes:', len(raw(p)))
PY
explanation: Scapy models protocol layers as Python objects.
options: The slash operator stacks layers. show displays fields; raw serializes them. This example has no send call and requires the Scapy package, not root privileges.
result: A local packet representation and length.

title: Nping: send three controlled TCP probes
explanation: Compare packet-level probing with a full application connection.
options: Start the listener first. Three SYN probes at one per second show response flags; the local kernel may issue resets because no matching normal TCP socket exists.
result: Reply timing and flags, not an authenticated session.

title: Hping3: compare a tiny SYN test
explanation: Craft a small TCP probe sequence for the same local port.
options: -S sets SYN, -p destination port, -c three packets, -i u1000000 a one-second interval. No reply is inconclusive; compare packet evidence and listener state.

title: iperf3: start a local measurement server
explanation: Prepare a server for one throughput test.
options: -B binds loopback, -p chooses the port, -1 exits after one client test. Run a client from another terminal.
result: A listener for a single test.

title: iperf3: run a bounded TCP test
explanation: Measure a three-second loopback transfer with a target rate of one megabit per second.
options: This measures local stack behavior, not the physical LAN speed. TCP throughput depends on endpoints and scheduling as well as links.

title: iperf3: observe UDP loss and jitter
explanation: Restart the one-shot server before running this separate exercise.
options: -u selects UDP data; iperf still uses a TCP control connection. Jitter is timing variation, distinct from latency; sender success does not prove all datagrams arrived.

title: DNS: query an owned lab resolver
explanation: Ask an explicitly configured lab DNS server about an example training zone.
options: Replace server and zone with your setup. A is an IPv4 record query. Inspect status and answer/authority sections; NXDOMAIN differs from timeout and from an empty successful answer.
result: A DNS response or bounded diagnostic.

title: DNS: compare TCP transport
explanation: Check the same question over TCP when diagnosing DNS transport behavior.
options: DNS needs more than UDP-only assumptions. Compare the same resolver and name. A transport difference may be caused by firewall policy rather than zone contents.

title: SMB: list shares with a test identity
explanation: Request a share list on a configured owned Samba or Windows lab server.
options: Enter the password at the prompt, not on the command line. A listed share is not proof of read or write access. Use the account and domain format required by your lab.
result: Shares allowed to be listed, or an authentication diagnostic.

title: SMB: test a permitted directory listing
explanation: Check read/list behavior inside one known training share.
options: The share must exist and contain synthetic data. Compare actual permissions to the role matrix; do not infer write permissions from a successful listing.
result: A directory listing or an access-denied response.

title: SNMP: read one object in a configured lab
explanation: Read sysUpTime from a lab agent configured with the fictional read-only community lab-readonly.
options: SNMPv2c communities are plaintext and command arguments can be visible locally. Use this only for the synthetic lab; use SNMPv3 authPriv for protected deployments. -r 0 avoids retries.
result: One uptime value or a timeout/access error.

title: SNMPv3: plan authenticated private access
command:
Confirm the SNMPv3 username and allowed object view.
Require authPriv and supported authentication/privacy algorithms.
Store credentials in a protected client configuration.
Read one permitted OID; confirm denied views separately.
explanation: SNMPv3 can provide authentication and encryption, but configuration determines both.
options: Do not assume that specifying version 3 automatically selects encryption. Use the installed Net-SNMP manual and device configuration to choose compatible algorithms. Keep real secrets out of shared notes.

title: SSH: audit advertised algorithms
explanation: Inspect the cryptographic configuration of a configured SSH lab service.
options: Check ssh-audit -h for your version. --skip-rate-test omits the connection-rate test in versions supporting it. This does not log in or prove that every advertised version has an unpatched flaw.

title: TLS: validate identity and chain
explanation: Connect to a TLS service configured for lab.test using your actual lab CA certificate.
options: SNI selects the virtual service; verify_hostname checks identity. verify_return_error stops on verification errors. The CA file and server must be configured separately; the HTTP practice server is not TLS.
result: Verification success or a specific certificate/protocol failure.

title: Review local firewall rules without changing them
explanation: Inspect the Linux nftables policy on your own Kali or lab server.
options: Trace the relevant family, hook, chain priority and rules in order. Containers and other firewall managers can add chains. An empty nftables view alone does not prove there is no filtering elsewhere.

title: Greenbone/OpenVAS: plan a focused scan
command:
Verify scanner readiness and feed synchronization.
Create a target containing one owned lab IP.
Review port list, credentials and scan configuration.
Run a bounded task and inspect the evidence behind each finding.
explanation: Greenbone provides vulnerability assessment workflows built around a scanner and management components.
options: Installation and feeds need separate resources. Authenticated checks can improve visibility; record whether authentication succeeded. Review test effects and exclude disruptive checks for the exercise.
result: A reviewed lab report with coverage limits.

title: Validate one network finding
command:
Record endpoint, protocol, time and scanner observation.
Confirm asset ownership and service configuration.
Check actual package/build and vendor remediation status.
Reproduce the smallest relevant behavior.
Retest after the configuration or patch change.
explanation: Reduce false positives before assigning remediation work.
options: A banner can conceal a backported security fix. Keep severity separate from confidence, and distinguish unreachable, untested and tested-negative states.
result: An evidence-backed finding and retest record.
